newsitem.title: GERMANY: Criticism rains down on Bonn for gold plan.
newsitem.headline: Criticism rains down on Bonn for gold plan.

text.p: German politicians and the press poured criticism on the government on Thursday for planning to override the respected Bundesbank and revalue its gold reserves to help Bonn qualify for Europe's single currency.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) demanded that Finance Minister Theo Waigel resign after his unprecedented clash with the central bank, and financial experts denounced the grab for gold as a threat to the euro currency Bonn wants to launch.

A Bundesbank council member, Ernst Welteke, even warned Chancellor Helmut Kohl he had failed to win public support for his pet project and that the Bundesbank would command more public sympathy than the politicians in an all-out clash.

But while the comments were negative, an undertone of resignation ran through them because the Bundesbank cannot prevent the reserves revaluation. Kohl has the majority to change the bank's laws to do it, and he made clear on Tuesday evening he would use his political power to get his way.

"The government's behaviour endangers what we need most urgently -- international credibility," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told the Berliner Zeitung. He called on Waigel to quit, saying: "The man is no longer tolerable".

Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf, a member of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), said Bonn should back down. Going ahead "means we won't have the authority we need to defend the independence of a European Central Bank".
Commentators warned that the gold plan was a high-risk gamble that threatened to destroy Germany's reputation for responsible economic policy.

"The government and the Bundesbank are on a confrontation course with an uncertain outcome," saud Germany's biggest newspaper, the popular Bild daily. "But one thing is sure -- there will be more than one bloody nose in this fight."

It said Germany's high-handed insistence that other Europeans refrain from budgetary tricks to qualify for EMU would now come back to haunt Bonn as it revalues the reserves to get a badly needed injection of cash.

"It is a classic conflict between the independent-minded protectors of the currency and the politicians who want to fill their empty state coffers," Bild said. "Bonn's obnoxious and loud insistence about the need for discipline will now come back to haunt it. It will be a painful awakening."
ARD television commented: "One gets the feeling that nothing and nobody is safe from Theo Waigel's creative budget practices.
"The political number jugglers can try to explain away a lot of things, but it is clear that they have lost touch with reality in Germany."
Hanover's Neue Presse called Waigel "a real Goldfinger". The Nuernberger Nachrichten said Kohl's government "is not only unable to solve our problems, it's part of the problem".

But, as the Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung pointed out, the Bundesbank's independence is based on a law that Kohl's majority in parliament can change to have the bank pay to Bonn the extra profit it would realise from revaluing its reserves.
"The thunder from the defenders of the currency in Frankfurt will probably have little effect, because they do not have a veto against laws that are passed," it wrote.
"If Waigel wants to take billions from the gold treasure, the government can change the Bundesbank law without even having to have the approval of the upper house of parliament."

The conservative Die Welt said in a page-one editorial headlined "The Lustre is Gone" that the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank had to raise objections to the government's plans or risk seeing its vaunted credibility in financial markets erode.
"Frankfurt is gluing together the porcelain which Bonn smashed," the Berlin-based daily said.
"However clever the gold trick may be, it is not a brilliant manoeuvre. The disdain with which other EU partners were treated due to their manipulation is now coming back to hit the Germans.
"The coalition has won money, but gambled away trust."
Countries wanting to enter European Monetary Union must have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
Bonn's figure for 1996 was 3.8 percent, and without the 20 billion marks ($11 billion) gained from the reserves there appears to be little chance Germany will qualify for EMU.
